heroLead: Montmorency County is thin on people and thick on state forest, but the Antrim Shale doesn't care about population, and a lot of families here still hold a mineral interest nobody's ever really explained to them.
intro: Atlanta is the county seat of Montmorency County, one of the least populated counties in the northern Lower Peninsula and also squarely inside the Antrim Shale core, alongside Otsego, Antrim, and Kalkaska counties. Big chunks of the county are state forest and hunting land now, but the mineral rights under a lot of that ground, and under the private farm and cabin parcels scattered through it, were leased and drilled during the Antrim boom of the late 1980s and 1990s.

We evaluate mineral and royalty interests across Montmorency County, from Atlanta and Hillman out to Lewiston and the resort development at Canada Creek Ranch. A lot of what we see here is small legacy interests, a handful of net mineral acres tied to family land that's been hunting camp or cabin property for two or three generations, with the mineral estate split off from the surface somewhere along the way.

sections.heading: Why this quiet county has real Antrim history
paragraphs: Montmorency County doesn't get talked about as much as some of its neighbors, but it was drilled hard during the Section 29 tax-credit years, same as the rest of the Antrim core. The formation here produces biogenic gas, generated by bacteria in the shale rather than heat and pressure, sitting shallow enough that dewatering the fracture network was necessary before gas would flow in volume.

Because so much of the county is public land and large private timber tracts, drilling patterns here can look a little different than the tighter residential spacing you'd see closer to Gaylord or Kalkaska, but the underlying geology and the mature, long-decline production behavior is the same story.

sections.heading: Ownership around hunting camps and family cabins
paragraphs: A huge share of private land in Montmorency County functions as recreational property, hunting camps and cabins passed down through families for generations. It's common for the mineral rights under that kind of property to have been reserved or sold separately from the surface decades ago, especially on tracts that changed hands multiple times through the 20th century.

That means you can own the cabin and the forty acres around it and have zero mineral interest in what's underneath, or you can be a fourth-generation heir getting a small royalty check on land your family sold the surface rights to years ago. Both show up regularly in Montmorency County, and the Montmorency County register of deeds in Atlanta is where the paper trail lives if you need to sort out which situation applies to you.

sections.heading: What a Montmorency County interest is realistically worth today
paragraphs: Same honest answer as the rest of the Antrim core: these wells are decades into a long, flat decline, and the volumes, and the checks, are a fraction of what they were at their 1990s peak. If your family's royalty statement shows a small number, that's not unusual for a mature biogenic gas well in this county, it's the expected shape of the curve this far out.

What we look at to price your interest is your actual current production and statements, net mineral acres, and any realistic chance of a workover or new activity nearby, not what the well made twenty-five years ago or a flat per-acre number pulled out of the air.

sections.heading: Working through unclear or clouded title
paragraphs: Given how much Montmorency County mineral ownership traces through multiple generations of heirship on rural and recreational land, it's common for title to be a little tangled, multiple heirs, missing probate records, or interests that were never formally divided. We've worked through that kind of title before and can walk you through what documentation you'll need before a sale can close cleanly.
If you're not sure whether you're the sole owner or one of several heirs, that's a normal starting point, not a dealbreaker. We'll help you figure out where you stand.

faqs.question: My family cabin is in Montmorency County but I've never gotten a royalty check. Do we own the minerals?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. A lot of surface property in this county was sold or inherited separately from the mineral rights underneath it. Check your deed language or pull the chain of title at the county register of deeds in Atlanta to see whether a prior owner reserved or sold the minerals separately.

faqs.question: Is there still active drilling in Montmorency County?
faqs.answer: Most current production is legacy Antrim Shale wells drilled during the 1980s and 1990s boom rather than new drilling. We check current operator activity specific to your section before quoting anything, since it varies across the county.

faqs.question: How do multiple heirs handle selling a shared mineral interest here?
faqs.answer: Each heir generally can sell their individual fractional share on their own, though clean probate or deed documentation showing how the interest was divided makes the process faster. We can help identify what paperwork you'll need.

faqs.question: Why does my Montmorency County royalty check seem so small compared to what I remember as a kid?
faqs.answer: If the well tied to your interest was drilled during the Antrim boom, it's now decades into a long, flat production decline. Biogenic shale gas wells keep producing a long time, but at steadily shrinking volumes, so today's check reflects a mature well, not a struggling one.

faqs.question: What's the first step to selling my Montmorency County mineral interest?
faqs.answer: Gather your deed or probate documentation and any royalty statements or division orders you have, then send them over for a real look. We'll tell you honestly what the interest is likely worth before you commit to anything.
